title: The Quid Pro Quo That Wasn’t
gist: Trump's mid-May 72-hour Beijing state visit, staged with a planeload of US tech, finance and consumer CEOs, produced goodwill declarations but no concrete opening of Chinese markets, deferring everything to a September 24 Trump-Xi meeting. The more consequential development was hidden in the May and June trade data: Chinese oil imports collapsed, and China's retreat from the seaborne crude market is why oil never spiked to the levels experts predicted after the Strait of Hormuz closure.

themes.theme: A summit that delivered optics, not deregulation

insights.claim: President Trump's mid-May 72-hour state visit to Beijing, accompanied by prominent American tech, finance and consumer-product CEOs, produced only broad declarations of goodwill and few concrete measures.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Investors who bought China-exposed US corporates on summit headlines were paying for optics; the market-opening trade has no policy backing yet.
insights.quote: In the end, aside from broad declarations of goodwill, few concrete measures were adopted.
insights.locator: In mid-May, and as the Strait of Hormuz closure

insights.claim: The composition of the delegation — CEOs of US tech, finance and consumer-product companies — was what generated market hopes for Chinese financial deregulation, wider market access for US firms and more cross-border investment, hopes that went unmet.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Treat delegation lists as a sentiment signal, not a policy signal; fade rallies in China-access names priced off attendee rosters.
insights.quote: The list of corporate leaders on the plane gave rise to hopes that China would embrace more financial deregulation, more market opening for US companies, and more cross-border investments.
insights.locator: President Trump was accompanied by many prominent American CEOs

insights.claim: Stabilization of the Sino-US relationship has been deferred to the scheduled September 24 meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, making that date the next binary catalyst for the bilateral relationship.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Mark September 24 as the event risk; positioning in China assets, tariffs-sensitive exporters and CNY should be sized around it rather than around summer headlines.
insights.quote: cans were kicked firmly down the road to the upcoming September 24 meeting between presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping
insights.locator: Instead, when it came to the stabilization of the Sino-US relationship

themes.theme: China's exit from the seaborne oil market

insights.claim: Chinese oil imports collapsed in the May and June trade data, with China essentially walking away from the global seaborne oil market.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: The marginal buyer of seaborne crude has stepped back; watch monthly Chinese customs import volumes as the key swing input for oil balances and tanker demand.
insights.quote: one important development was the collapse in Chinese oil imports that came through in the May and June trade data
insights.locator: Against this backdrop, one important development

insights.claim: The disappearance of Chinese seaborne crude buying is the reason oil prices failed to reach the levels most experts predicted would follow the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Demand destruction, not supply, is setting the oil price; long-oil geopolitical hedges can fail even with a closed chokepoint.
insights.quote: oil prices failed to reach the heights that most experts predicted would follow the Strait of Hormuz closure
insights.locator: With China essentially walking away from the global seaborne oil market

themes.theme: Consensus geopolitical risk models mispriced the chokepoint

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz had been closed for roughly ten weeks by mid-May without producing the oil price spike that most experts had forecast, showing that chokepoint-closure models overstate price impact when a major importer withdraws demand.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Reprice geopolitical oil hedges: supply-shock frameworks that ignore the demand response of the largest importer have been empirically wrong through this episode.
insights.quote: the Strait of Hormuz closure was entering its 10th week
insights.locator: In mid-May, and as the Strait of Hormuz closure

insights.claim: A prolonged Strait of Hormuz closure has not been enough to force a US-China grand bargain, as the two sides met at head-of-state level during the crisis and still adopted no concrete measures.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Do not assume energy-crisis urgency compresses the US-China negotiating timeline; deals slip even under acute stress.
insights.locator: Instead, when it came to the stabilization of the Sino-US relationship
